clinicalPearls: NTS infection most often produces a gastroenteritis that is clinically indistinguishable from that caused by other enteric pathogens, with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea beginning 6-48 h after ingestion of contaminated food or water; stools are usually loose, nonbloody, and of moderate volume, though large-volume watery stools, bloody stools, or frank dysentery can occur (p.1320).
NTS gastroenteritis is usually self-limited: diarrhea resolves within 3-7 days and fever within 72 h; stool cultures may remain positive for 4-5 weeks after infection (p.1320).

Globally S. Typhimurium and S. Enteritidis are the most common serotypes causing human disease; in the United States NTS is the second most common cause of foodborne outbreaks after norovirus (p.1319).

Unlike S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi (human-only reservoir), NTS is acquired from multiple animal and plant reservoirs - especially eggs, poultry, undercooked ground meat, and dairy, plus produce contaminated with animal waste and contact with animals (reptiles, amphibians, chicks, etc.) (p.1319).

Up to 8% of patients with NTS gastroenteritis develop bacteremia, and of those 5-10% develop localized (metastatic) infections; bacteremia and metastatic infection are most common with S. Choleraesuis and S. Dublin and among infants, the elderly, and the immunocompromised, especially those with HIV (p.1320).

Invasive NTS disease (predominantly S. Typhimurium ST313 and S. Enteritidis ST11) is a leading cause of bacteremia in children and HIV-infected adults in sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia; it typically presents as a nonspecific febrile illness resembling enteric fever and uncommonly causes diarrhea (p.1319-1320).

Diagnosis rests on isolating the organism from freshly passed stool or from blood or another normally sterile fluid; culture-independent molecular tests are increasingly used but positive specimens should still undergo primary isolation, and all NTS isolates should be referred to public health for serotyping (p.1320-1321).
Reactive arthritis can follow NTS gastroenteritis, occurring most frequently in persons carrying the HLA-B27 antigen (p.1321).

Localized NTS infections include intraabdominal (hepatic/splenic abscess, cholecystitis), CNS (meningitis - chiefly in infants 1-4 months and HIV-infected adults), pulmonary (lobar pneumonia), urinary/genital, and bone/joint disease; Salmonella osteomyelitis classically affects the femur, tibia, humerus, or lumbar vertebrae and is strongly linked to sickle cell disease and hemoglobinopathies (p.1320-1321).
harrison.pathophysiology: All Salmonella infections begin with ingestion of organisms, usually in contaminated food or water; the infectious dose ranges from ~200 to 10^6 CFU, and the ingested dose helps determine incubation period and severity. Conditions reducing gastric acidity (age <1 year, acid-suppression therapy, achlorhydria) or compromising intestinal integrity (inflammatory bowel disease, cytotoxic chemotherapy, prior GI surgery, antibiotic-induced microbiome alteration) increase susceptibility. In contrast to enteric fever (mononuclear infiltration of small-bowel mucosa), NTS gastroenteritis is characterized by massive polymorphonuclear leukocyte infiltration into both large- and small-bowel mucosa. This response depends largely on induction of interleukin 8, a strong neutrophil chemoattractant secreted by intestinal cells in response to NTS colonization and translocation of bacterial proteins and LPS into host cytoplasm with subsequent inflammasome activation; neutrophil degranulation and release of toxic substances damages the mucosa, producing inflammatory diarrhea. NTS persistence is aided by its ability to use tetrathionate (generated from thiosulfate via inflammatory reactive oxygen species) for metabolism in a microaerophilic, inflamed gut, allowing it to outcompete endogenous flora. Unlike typhoidal serotypes, NTS effectively colonizes the intestinal tract rather than evolving as a primarily systemic pathogen.

harrison.prognosis: NTS gastroenteritis is usually self-limited, with diarrhea resolving in 3-7 days and fever within 72 h; chronic carriage develops in <1% of cases. Outcomes worsen markedly with invasive disease: endocarditis and arteritis are rare (<1%) but carry serious, potentially fatal complications (valve perforation, endomyocardial abscess, infected mural thrombus, pericarditis, mycotic aneurysm, aneurysm rupture, aortoenteric fistula, vertebral osteomyelitis), and NTS meningitis is fatal in up to 60% of cases. In 2017 there were ~535,000 invasive NTS cases and ~77,500 deaths worldwide, ~80% in sub-Saharan Africa. Acute NTS gastroenteritis was associated with a threefold increased risk of dyspepsia and irritable bowel syndrome at 1 year in a Spanish study.
pitfalls: Antibiotics should NOT be used routinely to treat uncomplicated NTS gastroenteritis - the illness is usually self-limited and antibiotics do not significantly shorten fever or diarrhea, while they have been associated with increased relapse rates, prolonged fecal/gastrointestinal carriage, and adverse drug reactions.
Only ~1% of clinical isolates ferment lactose, so a high index of suspicion is needed to detect rare lactose-fermenting strains.

Decreased-ciprofloxacin-susceptibility NTS strains may not be reliably detected by nalidixic acid susceptibility testing or standard ciprofloxacin disk diffusion, risking missed resistance and treatment failure.

Neonates, the elderly, and immunosuppressed patients with NTS gastroenteritis are especially prone to dehydration and invasive infection and may need hospitalization and antibiotic therapy - they are exceptions to the no-routine-antibiotics rule.
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison does not provide a formal graded severity score for NTS. Disease is described along a clinical spectrum: (1) uncomplicated self-limited gastroenteritis; (2) bacteremia (low-grade defined as <50% of blood cultures positive vs high-grade >50% of three or more sets positive, the latter raising concern for endovascular infection); and (3) localized/metastatic infection (intraabdominal, CNS, pulmonary, urinary/genital, bone/joint/soft tissue) and endovascular infection (endocarditis, arteritis). Host-risk stratification for invasive disease includes neonates (up to ~3 months), persons >50 years with atherosclerosis, and those with immunosuppression, cardiac valvular/endovascular abnormalities, or significant joint disease.
